chapters.name: Chapter 1: Numbers you use every day

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Fractions, decimals, percents and the tape measure
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Convert between fractions, decimals and percents and read a tape measure.
This lesson builds toward: Given fractions, decimals, percents and a tape measure, you will convert between fractions, decimals and percents and read a tape measure to the nearest 1/8 inch, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Fractions, decimals and percents are three ways to write the same amount. Half a pizza is 1/2, or 0.5, or 50%. A quarter is 1/4, 0.25 or 25%. Three quarters is 3/4, 0.75 or 75%.
To change a fraction into a decimal, divide the top number by the bottom number: 3/8 is 3 divided by 8, which is 0.375. To change a decimal into a percent, move the decimal point two places to the right: 0.375 is 37.5%. To go from a percent to a decimal, move it two places to the left: 15% is 0.15.
A tape measure in the US shows inches split into 16 small marks. The longest mark in the middle of an inch is 1/2. The next longest marks are 1/4 and 3/4. Then 1/8, 3/8, 5/8 and 7/8. The shortest are sixteenths. If the tape stops 3 marks of 1/8 past the 5, it reads 5 and 3/8 inches.
Adding fractions with the same bottom number is easy: add the tops and keep the bottom. 1/8 + 3/8 = 4/8, which is the same as 1/2.
Step by step:
- Fraction to decimal: divide top by bottom.
- Decimal to percent: move the point 2 places right.
- Percent to decimal: move the point 2 places left.
- Tape measure: find the whole inch, then count the marks past it.
- Simplify: 4/8 is the same as 1/2.
Words to know:
- Fraction: a part of a whole, written as top number over bottom number, like 3/4.
- Numerator: the top number of a fraction: how many parts you have.
- Denominator: the bottom number of a fraction: how many equal parts make a whole.
- Decimal: a number with a point, like 0.75, that shows parts of a whole.
- Percent (%): parts out of 100. 25% means 25 out of 100.
Try it now: Practice (answers below): (1) Write 1/4 as a decimal and a percent. (2) Write 0.6 as a percent. (3) Write 8% as a decimal. (4) Change 5/8 to a decimal. (5) Add 1/4 + 1/4. Answers: (1) 0.25 and 25%; (2) 60%; (3) 0.08; (4) 0.625; (5) 2/4, which is 1/2. If you have a tape measure or ruler, measure 3 things at home to the nearest 1/8 inch.
You can now switch between fractions, decimals and percents and read a tape measure to the nearest 1/8 inch.

check.why: 3 divided by 4 is 0.75, and moving the point two places right gives 75%.
Move the point two places left: 6% = 0.06.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Discounts, sales tax, tips and raises
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate discounts, sales tax, tips and raises with percents.
This lesson builds toward: Given a price, a bill or a pay rate, you will calculate a discount, sales tax, a tip or a raise using percents, to the nearest cent.
To find a percent of a number, change the percent to a decimal and multiply. 20% of $45 is 0.20 x 45 = $9.
Discount: subtract it from the price. A $45 jacket at 20% off costs 45 - 9 = $36. Sales tax: add it on. If the tax rate is 8%, the tax on $36 is 0.08 x 36 = $2.88, so you pay $38.88. Sales tax rates are different in each state and city; check your state's tax agency or look at a receipt.
Tip without a calculator: find 10% by moving the point one place left, then build from it. On a $28 bill, 10% is $2.80, 5% is half of that, $1.40, so 15% is $2.80 + $1.40 = $4.20. 20% is double 10%: $5.60.
Raise: a 3% raise on $16.00 an hour is 0.03 x 16 = $0.48, so the new rate is $16.48 an hour. Watch the words: "20% off" means you pay 80% of the price; "20% more" means you pay 120%.
Step by step:
- Change the percent to a decimal.
- Multiply by the amount.
- Discount: subtract. Tax or tip: add. Raise: add to the old rate.
- Round money to the nearest cent.
- Check: does the answer make sense? A discount must be less than the price.
Words to know:
- Discount: money taken off the price.
- Sales tax: a tax added to the price at the register; the rate depends on your state and city.
- Tip: extra money you give for service, often figured as a percent of the bill.
- Raise: an increase in your pay rate.
- Round: make a number simpler; money is rounded to the nearest cent.
Official sources:
- Federation of Tax Administrators: State tax agency links
Try it now: Practice (answers below): (1) A $60 pair of work boots is 25% off. What is the sale price? (2) Tax is 7% on a $50 item. What is the total? (3) Find a 20% tip on a $35 bill. (4) Your $15.50 pay rate gets a 4% raise. What is the new rate? Answers: (1) $45; (2) $3.50 tax, $53.50 total; (3) $7.00; (4) $0.62 more, $16.12 an hour. Then look at a real receipt and find the tax rate your area charged.
You can now figure discounts, sales tax, tips and raises to the nearest cent.

check.q: A $80 coat is 25% off. What is the sale price?
What is a 15% tip on a $40 bill?

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Unit prices: finding the better buy
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Calculate unit prices and choose the better buy.
This lesson builds toward: Given two sizes of the same product and their prices, you will calculate each unit price and choose the better buy, choosing correctly in at least 4 of 5 pairs.
A unit price is the cost for one unit: one ounce, one pound, one count. It lets you compare different sizes fairly. To find it, divide the price by the number of units.
Example: a 24-ounce box of cereal costs $4.80. $4.80 / 24 = $0.20 an ounce. A 36-ounce box costs $6.12. $6.12 / 36 = $0.17 an ounce. The bigger box is the better buy.
Bigger is not always cheaper. A 2-pound bag of rice for $3.18 is $1.59 a pound. A 5-pound bag for $8.45 is $1.69 a pound. Here the small bag is the better buy. Many stores print the unit price in small type on the shelf tag; check that both tags use the same unit.
The better buy is only better if you will use it before it goes bad and you can afford it this week. Unit prices also help at work, for example when ordering supplies.
Step by step:
- Write the price and the size of each item.
- Make sure the units match (ounces with ounces).
- Divide: price / size = unit price.
- Compare: the lower unit price is the better buy.
- Ask: will I use it all, and can I afford it now?
Words to know:
- Unit price: the cost for one unit, like one ounce or one pound.
- Ounce (oz): a small unit of weight; 16 ounces make 1 pound.
- Pound (lb): a unit of weight equal to 16 ounces.
- Shelf tag: the price label on the store shelf; it often shows the unit price.
Try it now: Practice (answers below): (1) 12 eggs for $3.60 or 18 eggs for $5.04? (2) 64 oz of juice for $3.84 or 128 oz for $6.40? Answers: (1) $0.30 an egg vs $0.28 an egg: 18 eggs is better; (2) $0.06 an ounce vs $0.05 an ounce: 128 oz is better. Then, at a store or on a store's website, find the unit prices of 3 things you buy often in two sizes and write down the better buy. This goes on your final task sheet.
You can now find unit prices and pick the better buy, and know when the bigger size is not worth it.

check.q: A 10-pound bag of potatoes costs $5.90. What is the unit price?
Soap A: 3 bars for $2.70. Soap B: 8 bars for $8.00. Which is the better buy?
options: Soap B, because it has more bars
They cost the same per bar
Soap B, because it costs more
Soap A, at $0.90 a bar vs $1.00
check.why: $2.70 / 3 = $0.90 and $8.00 / 8 = $1.00, so A costs less per bar.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Math for work and money

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Measuring, converting and counting work hours
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Convert units and calculate area and hours worked for a work task.
This lesson builds toward: Given a work task such as flooring a room or logging a shift, you will convert units and calculate area or hours worked, with the right unit, and rounding up when you need whole items.
Common US units: 12 inches = 1 foot, 3 feet = 1 yard, 16 ounces = 1 pound, 2 pints = 1 quart, 4 quarts = 1 gallon. Some jobs use metric: 1 inch = 2.54 centimeters, and 1 kilogram is about 2.2 pounds. To change a big unit into small units, multiply; to change small units into big units, divide. 90 inches / 12 = 7.5 feet.
Area is the space a flat surface covers: length x width, in square units. A room 12 feet by 10 feet is 12 x 10 = 120 square feet. If one box of flooring covers 20 square feet, you need 120 / 20 = 6 boxes. Workers often add about 10% extra for cuts and mistakes: 120 x 1.10 = 132, and 132 / 20 = 6.6. You cannot buy 0.6 of a box, so round UP to 7.
Hours worked: count from start to end, then take out unpaid breaks. A shift from 7:30 am to 4:00 pm is 8 1/2 hours; minus a 30-minute unpaid lunch is 8 hours. Many timecards use decimal hours: 15 minutes = 0.25, 30 minutes = 0.5, 45 minutes = 0.75. Some workplaces use a 24-hour clock: 15:00 is 3:00 pm.
Step by step:
- Write what you have and the unit you need.
- Big to small unit: multiply. Small to big: divide.
- Area: length x width, in square units.
- Need whole items (boxes, bags): always round up.
- Hours: end time minus start time, minus unpaid breaks; change minutes to decimals by dividing by 60.
Words to know:
- Unit: what you measure in, like inches, feet, pounds or hours.
- Convert: change a measurement from one unit to another.
- Area: the space a flat surface covers: length times width, in square units.
- Square feet (sq ft): the unit for area when you measure in feet.
- Metric: the measuring system used in most of the world: centimeters, meters, kilograms, liters.
- Decimal hours: time written as a decimal, like 7.75 hours for 7 hours 45 minutes.
Try it now: Practice (answers below): (1) Change 5 feet to inches. (2) Change 48 ounces to pounds. (3) A storage room is 9 feet by 14 feet. What is the area? (4) Paint covers about 350 square feet a gallon (on this made-up can). You must cover 800 square feet. How many gallons do you buy? (5) You work 6:45 am to 3:15 pm with a 30-minute unpaid lunch. How many hours, as a decimal? Answers: (1) 60 inches; (2) 3 pounds; (3) 126 square feet; (4) 800 / 350 = 2.29, so buy 3 gallons; (5) 8.5 hours minus 0.5 = 8.0 hours.
You can now convert units, find area, round up for whole items and count your work hours as decimals.

check.q: You need 4.2 bags of concrete mix. How many bags do you buy?
check.why: You cannot buy part of a bag, so round up to 5.

check.q: How many hours is 7 hours and 45 minutes as a decimal?

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Checking your paystub
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check the hours, rate, overtime, deductions and net pay on a paystub.
This lesson builds toward: Given a paystub, you will check the hours, pay rate, overtime, deductions and net pay line by line, with every line matching to the cent, or the mistake written down to ask about.
A paystub shows how your pay was figured. Gross pay is what you earned before anything is taken out. Deductions are amounts taken out, such as taxes. Net pay is what you actually get: gross pay minus deductions. YTD means year to date: the total so far this year.
Practice paystub (made up): 45 hours at $18.00 an hour. Under federal law, covered hourly workers get overtime for hours over 40 in a workweek, at least time and a half. So: 40 x $18.00 = $720.00 regular pay. Overtime rate is $18.00 x 1.5 = $27.00, and 5 x $27.00 = $135.00. Gross pay = $855.00. Some states have extra overtime rules; check your state labor office.
Deductions on this stub: Social Security 6.2% of $855.00 = $53.01. Medicare 1.45% = $12.40. Federal income tax $60.00 and state tax $20.00 (these depend on your W-4 form and your state; they are made up here). Total deductions = $145.41. Net pay = $855.00 - $145.41 = $709.59.
If a line is wrong, write down the pay date, the line and what you expected, then ask payroll or your supervisor first. If it is not fixed, you can contact your state labor office or the U.S. Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division. Keep your paystubs, and cover your Social Security number before showing one to anyone.
Step by step:
- Check the hours against your own record of the hours you worked.
- Regular pay: up to 40 hours x your rate.
- Overtime: hours over 40 x (rate x 1.5), if you are covered.
- Gross pay = regular pay + overtime + any other pay.
- Add up all the deductions.
- Net pay = gross pay - total deductions. Does it match the stub?
- If not, write it down and ask payroll.
Words to know:
- Paystub: the paper or online record that shows how your pay was figured.
- Gross pay: what you earned before anything is taken out.
- Net pay: what you take home after deductions; also called take-home pay.
- Deduction: an amount taken out of your pay, like taxes or insurance.
- Overtime: extra pay, at least 1.5 times your rate, for covered hours over 40 in a workweek under federal law.
- YTD (year to date): the total from January 1 up to this paycheck.
- W-4: the form you give your employer that sets how much federal income tax is withheld.
Official sources:
- U.S. Department of Labor: Overtime pay
- IRS Topic 751: Social Security and Medicare withholding rates
Try it now: Practice (answers below): You worked 42 hours at $16.00 an hour. Deductions: Social Security 6.2%, Medicare 1.45%, federal tax $45.00, state tax $15.00 (made up). Find (1) regular pay, (2) overtime pay, (3) gross pay, (4) total deductions, (5) net pay. Answers: (1) $640.00; (2) 2 x $24.00 = $48.00; (3) $688.00; (4) $42.66 + $9.98 + $45.00 + $15.00 = $112.64; (5) $575.36. Then check a real paystub of your own the same way, with private numbers covered.
You can now check every line of a paystub and know what to do if something does not add up.

check.q: Gross pay is $600.00 and deductions total $95.00. What is net pay?
You earn $20.00 an hour and are covered by federal overtime. What is your overtime rate?

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Building a monthly budget from your pay
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a monthly budget with savings that keeps spending at or below income.
This lesson builds toward: Given a regular paycheck, you will build a monthly budget that includes savings and keeps spending at or below income, with every category written down and the totals checked.
A budget is a plan for your money. Start with monthly take-home (net) pay. Months are a little longer than 4 weeks, so do not just multiply weekly pay by 4. Paid weekly: weekly net x 52 / 12. Paid every two weeks: net x 26 / 12. Example: $700 a week x 52 = $36,400 a year, / 12 = $3,033.33 a month.
List your spending: needs first (rent, utilities, food, transportation, phone, child care, minimum debt payments), then savings, then wants. Example: rent $1,200, utilities $150, phone $50, food $400, transportation $200, debt $150, savings $150. That totals $2,300, which leaves $733.33 for other needs and wants.
The rule: total spending (including savings) must be equal to or less than income. If it is more, cut a want, lower a bill, or find more income. Check the totals by adding them a second time, or with a calculator.
Track it for one month. Write down what you really spend, then compare with your plan and adjust. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's free "Your Money, Your Goals" materials have worksheets you can print.
Step by step:
- Find monthly take-home pay (weekly x 52 / 12, or every-two-weeks x 26 / 12).
- List needs: rent, utilities, food, transportation, phone, child care, debt minimums.
- Add a savings line, even a small one.
- Add wants last.
- Total spending must be at or below income.
- Track for a month and adjust.
Words to know:
- Budget: a plan for how you will use your money each month.
- Income: money coming in, like your take-home pay.
- Expense: money going out, like rent or groceries.
- Fixed expense: an expense that is the same each month, like rent.
- Variable expense: an expense that changes each month, like food or gas.
Official sources:
- CFPB: Your Money, Your Goals (free budgeting materials)
Try it now: Finish your final task. Use the net pay from your Lesson 5 paystub (or your own) and turn it into monthly income. Write a budget with needs, a savings line and wants. Add it up twice. If spending is more than income, change it until it fits. Put your paystub check, budget and 3 unit-price comparisons on one page: your "Work and Money Math Sheet".
You can now turn a paycheck into monthly income and build a budget that balances and includes savings.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Paystub checked Some lines not checked, or math errors in gross or net pay. Hours, rate, overtime, deductions and net pay checked; every line matches to the cent or a mistake is written down. Also writes what to say to payroll about any mistake and where to go next. Monthly income Weekly pay multiplied by 4, or gross pay used instead of net. Monthly take-home pay found with x 52 / 12 or x 26 / 12. Shows the work and checks it a second way. Balanced budget Spending is more than income, or there is no savings line. Needs, savings and wants listed; spending at or below income; totals checked. Includes a plan to track real spending and a date to review it. Unit prices Fewer than 3 comparisons, or units do not match. 3 comparisons with correct unit prices and the better buy marked. Notes when the bigger size is not the better choice and why. Percents Practice answers for discounts, tax, tips or raises are often wrong. At least 4 of 5 percent practice problems right, to the cent. Can explain the shortcut (10%, then build) to someone else. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, redo that part with the lesson's steps and check it again.

check.q: You take home $500 a week. What is your monthly income?
check.why: $500 x 52 / 12 = $2,166.67; multiplying by 4 leaves out the extra days.

check.q: Your planned spending is $50 more than your income. What do you do?
options: Remove the savings line and ignore it
Use a payday loan every month
Cut or lower some expenses until spending fits
check.why: A budget only works when spending is at or below income.
